Example 6.70

The lower curve of tangent and cotangent

Sketch h(x)=min{tanx,cotx}h(x)=\min\{\tan x,\cot x\}.

Solution.

Start with the common domain. Tangent requires cosx≠0\cos x\ne0, and cotangent requires sinx≠0\sin x\ne0. Therefore D=ℝ\{kπ2:k∈ℤ}.D=\mathbb{R}\setminus\left\{\frac{k\pi}{2}:k\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}. Although one of the two functions may be defined at an excluded input, their minimum is not defined there. For example, tan0=0\tan0=0, but cot0\cot0 does not exist, so h(0)h(0) does not exist.

On DD, their intersections satisfy tanx=cotx=1tanx⇔tan2x=1⇔x=π4+kπ2.\tan x=\cot x=\frac1{\tan x} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \tan^2x=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\frac\pi4+\frac{k\pi}{2}. The intersection heights alternate between 11 and −1-1.

It is enough to analyse 0<x<π0<x<\pi, because both candidate functions repeat after π\pi. On (0,π/2)(0,\pi/2), both are positive. The smaller is tangent up to π/4\pi/4, then cotangent. On (π/2,π)(\pi/2,\pi), both are negative. Just to the right of π/2\pi/2, tangent is very negative and is the smaller value; just to the left of π\pi, cotangent is very negative and is the smaller value. The switch is at 3π/43\pi/4, where both equal −1-1. Thus, for every integer nn, h(x)={tanx,nπ<x≤nπ+π/4,cotx,nπ+π/4<x<nπ+π/2,tanx,nπ+π/2<x≤nπ+3π/4,cotx,nπ+3π/4<x<(n+1)π.h(x)=\begin{cases} \tan x,&n\pi<x\leq n\pi+\pi/4,\\ \cot x,&n\pi+\pi/4<x<n\pi+\pi/2,\\ \tan x,&n\pi+\pi/2<x\leq n\pi+3\pi/4,\\ \cot x,&n\pi+3\pi/4<x<(n+1)\pi. \end{cases} On the positive pieces the values lie in (0,1](0,1]; on the negative pieces they lie in (−∞,−1](-\infty,-1]. Hence range(h)=(−∞,−1]∪(0,1].\operatorname{range}(h)=(-\infty,-1]\cup(0,1]. The value 00 is never attained, even where a branch approaches the horizontal axis.

Notice that a half-period shift does not preserve this graph: positive pieces become negative pieces. The graph repeats after π\pi.

Example 6.71

Distance to the nearest of three points

Sketch h(x)=min{|x|,|x−1|,|x+1|}h(x)=\min\{|x|,|x-1|,|x+1|\}.

Solution.

The three candidate values are the distances from xx to 0,1,−10,1,-1, respectively. Taking the minimum means measuring the distance to the nearest of these three points. All three expressions are defined for every real input.

The midpoint between −1-1 and 00 is −1/2-1/2. To its left, −1-1 is nearer; to its right, 00 is nearer until the midpoint 1/21/2. Beyond 1/21/2, the point 11 is nearest. Therefore h(x)={|x+1|,x≤−1/2,|x|,−1/2<x≤1/2,|x−1|,x>1/2.h(x)=\begin{cases} |x+1|,&x\leq-1/2,\\ |x|,&-1/2<x\leq1/2,\\ |x-1|,&x>1/2. \end{cases} We have chosen the nearest point, but each distance still contains an absolute value. Split again where its inside expression changes sign: at −1,0,1-1,0,1. This gives the six straight pieces h(x)={−x−1,x≤−1,x+1,−1<x≤−1/2,−x,−1/2<x≤0,x,0<x≤1/2,1−x,1/2<x≤1,x−1,x>1.h(x)=\begin{cases} -x-1,&x\leq-1,\\ x+1,&-1<x\leq-1/2,\\ -x,&-1/2<x\leq0,\\ x,&0<x\leq1/2,\\ 1-x,&1/2<x\leq1,\\ x-1,&x>1. \end{cases} Adjacent formulas agree at every joining point. Thus all five corners belong to the graph.

The function is even: reflecting xx to −x-x interchanges the distances to −1-1 and 11, while leaving the distance to 00 unchanged. Its domain is ℝ\mathbb{R}, and its range is [0,∞)[0,\infty). The two middle peaks have height 1/21/2, but they are not a greatest value of the whole function: the outer rays grow without bound.

6.18 Adding Graphs: A Curve Between Two Boundaries

The sum h(x)=f(x)+g(x)h(x)=f(x)+g(x) adds vertical coordinates at the same input. For instance, if the two points above x=2x=2 have heights 55 and −3-3, then the new height is 22. We neither add the inputs nor join the two graphs together. The domain of the sum is Df∩DgD_f\cap D_g.

Suppose that a≤g(x)≤ba\leq g(x)\leq b throughout this common domain. Adding f(x)f(x) to each part preserves both inequalities: f(x)+a≤f(x)+g(x)≤f(x)+b.f(x)+a\leq f(x)+g(x)\leq f(x)+b. Thus the graph lies between two vertical translates of ff. The bounds need not be attained; equality occurs only where g(x)=ag(x)=a or g(x)=bg(x)=b. The following checks locate the graph inside that strip: Value of g(x)Value of h(x)Position relative to y=f(x)g(x)=0h(x)=f(x)on the reference curveg(x)>0h(x)>f(x)above itg(x)<0h(x)<f(x)below it\begin{array}{c|c|l} \text{Value of }g(x)&\text{Value of }h(x)&\text{Position relative to }y=f(x)\\ \hline g(x)=0&h(x)=f(x)&\text{on the reference curve}\\ g(x)>0&h(x)>f(x)&\text{above it}\\ g(x)<0&h(x)<f(x)&\text{below it} \end{array} Bounds give a useful framework, but do not determine a unique curve. Intercepts, signs, symmetry and, where needed, monotonicity supply the remaining information.

Example 6.72

An oscillation around a straight line

Sketch h(x)=x+sinxh(x)=x+\sin x.

Solution.

Since −1≤sinx≤1-1\leq\sin x\leq1, we have x−1≤h(x)≤x+1.x-1\leq h(x)\leq x+1. Draw y=xy=x as the reference line and y=x−1,y=x+1y=x-1,\ y=x+1 as its two boundaries. At x=nπx=n\pi, the sine term is zero, so the curve passes through (nπ,nπ)(n\pi,n\pi). It reaches the upper boundary when x=π/2+2nπx=\pi/2+2n\pi, and the lower boundary when x=3π/2+2nπx=3\pi/2+2n\pi. For example, x−3π/2−π−π/20π/2π3π/2h(x)−3π/2+1−π−π/2−10π/2+1π3π/2−1\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr} x&-3\pi/2&-\pi&-\pi/2&0&\pi/2&\pi&3\pi/2\\ \hline h(x)&-3\pi/2+1&-\pi&-\pi/2-1&0&\pi/2+1&\pi&3\pi/2-1 \end{array} The sine term is positive on (2nπ,(2n+1)π)(2n\pi,(2n+1)\pi), so the graph is above y=xy=x there. It is negative on ((2n−1)π,2nπ)((2n-1)\pi,2n\pi), so the graph is below y=xy=x there.

Interactive graph

Trace the sum between its bounds

f(x) = x
ParentTransformedGuide

Both summands are odd, so hh is odd. Its domain and range are both ℝ\mathbb{R}. For the range, the two envelope lines force the graph arbitrarily high on the right and arbitrarily low on the left. Reading its unbroken curve by the crossing picture gives every intermediate height; continuity will justify that reading in Calculus.

After the Calculus module: does the graph ever turn downward? The following derivative check is optional on a first reading. Using the slope criterion from Lecture 5's later-reading section, h′(x)=1+cosx≥0.h'(x)=1+\cos x\geq0. Thus the function is nondecreasing. The derivative vanishes only at the isolated inputs (2n+1)π(2n+1)\pi, so it cannot be constant on any nontrivial interval. A nondecreasing function with equal values at two distinct inputs would be constant between them. Consequently hh is in fact strictly increasing. Its horizontal tangents are flat moments of an increasing curve, not local maxima or minima.

Back to the graphical reading: repeated translated stretches. The sine term repeats, but the whole function does not: h(x+2π)=h(x)+2π.h(x+2\pi)=h(x)+2\pi. Each successive stretch is translated by (2π,2π)(2\pi,2\pi).

6.19 Multiplying Graphs: Amplitude and Envelopes

For a product h(x)=f(x)g(x)h(x)=f(x)g(x), we again work at the same input, in the common domain. If a≤g(x)≤ba\leq g(x)\leq b, the sign of f(x)f(x) decides the order of the new bounds: af(x)≤f(x)g(x)≤bf(x),when f(x)≥0,bf(x)≤f(x)g(x)≤af(x),when f(x)<0.\begin{array}{ll} af(x)\leq f(x)g(x)\leq bf(x),&\text{when }f(x)\geq0,\\[2pt] bf(x)\leq f(x)g(x)\leq af(x),&\text{when }f(x)<0. \end{array} For example, multiplying −1≤sinx≤1-1\leq\sin x\leq1 by a negative xx reverses both inequalities. A formula that automatically handles both signs is min{af(x),bf(x)}≤f(x)g(x)≤max{af(x),bf(x)}.\min\{af(x),bf(x)\}\leq f(x)g(x)\leq\max\{af(x),bf(x)\}. (6.2) In particular, whenever |g(x)|≤1|g(x)|\leq1, −|f(x)|≤f(x)g(x)≤|f(x)|.-|f(x)|\leq f(x)g(x)\leq|f(x)|. The two bounding curves are called envelopes here: they provide an upper and lower outline within which the oscillation fits. An envelope need not itself be part of the graph, and a contact with it need not be a local maximum or minimum of the product.

💡 Multiplication and the order of two values

For real numbers u,v,cu,v,c, min{cu,cv}={cmin{u,v},c≥0,cmax{u,v},c<0,\min\{cu,cv\}=\begin{cases}c\min\{u,v\},&c\geq0,\\c\max\{u,v\},&c<0,\end{cases} and max{cu,cv}={cmax{u,v},c≥0,cmin{u,v},c<0.\max\{cu,cv\}=\begin{cases}c\max\{u,v\},&c\geq0,\\c\min\{u,v\},&c<0.\end{cases} A negative multiplier interchanges “higher” and “lower.” The same statement applies point by point when the multiplier depends on xx.

To locate a product inside its envelopes, mark every zero of either factor that belongs to the common domain. Between these zeros, use the signs of both factors: equal signs give a positive product; opposite signs give a negative product. Then locate the points where a bound is attained. These data usually make the shape much clearer than a large table of arbitrary values.

Example 6.73

An oscillation with growing amplitude

Sketch h(x)=xsinxh(x)=x\sin x.

Solution.

Because |sinx|≤1|\sin x|\leq1, |xsinx|≤|x|,or equivalently−|x|≤h(x)≤|x|.|x\sin x|\leq|x|, \qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad -|x|\leq h(x)\leq|x|. The two straight lines y=xy=x and y=−xy=-x therefore bound the oscillation; their roles as upper and lower boundary exchange at 00. On x≥0x\geq0, the inequalities read −x≤h(x)≤x-x\leq h(x)\leq x. On x<0x<0, they read x≤h(x)≤−xx\leq h(x)\leq-x.

The zeros are exactly x=nπx=n\pi, n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. The graph is even, since h(−x)=(−x)sin(−x)=xsinx=h(x).h(-x)=(-x)\sin(-x)=x\sin x=h(x). Thus we can construct the right half first and reflect it in the vertical axis. For x>0x>0, its sign is the sign of sinx\sin x: the first lobe is positive, the next negative, and so on. At the origin, the function is positive on both nearby sides, so it touches the axis there. At every other zero it changes sign and crosses the axis.

The contact points with the two straight lines are given by sinx=1⇒h(x)=x,x=π/2+2nπ,sinx=−1⇒h(x)=−x,x=3π/2+2nπ.\begin{array}{lll} \sin x=1&\Longrightarrow h(x)=x,&x=\pi/2+2n\pi,\\ \sin x=-1&\Longrightarrow h(x)=-x,&x=3\pi/2+2n\pi. \end{array} These formulas include negative integers nn as well as nonnegative ones.

The domain is ℝ\mathbb{R}, and the range is also ℝ\mathbb{R}. Indeed, at positive inputs with sinx=1\sin x=1, the values grow without bound; at positive inputs with sinx=−1\sin x=-1, they become arbitrarily negative. The familiar unbroken lobes pass through the heights between these values, by the graphical crossing picture. The formal continuity justification is reserved for the Calculus module. The increasing size of the lobes shows that the product is not periodic.

Example 6.74

An oscillation with shrinking amplitude

Sketch h(x)=sinx/xh(x)=\sin x/x.

Solution.

Domain first. The given quotient is defined on ℝ\{0}\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}. No cancellation gives it a value at 00, since sinx\sin x is not the factor xx. For every nonzero input, |sinxx|≤1|x|,−1|x|≤h(x)≤1|x|.\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\leq\frac1{|x|}, \qquad -\frac1{|x|}\leq h(x)\leq\frac1{|x|}. The curves y=1/xy=1/x and y=−1/xy=-1/x form the two boundaries; on the negative half-axis their upper and lower roles are reversed. The envelopes become unbounded near 00, but this does not mean that the graph of hh does. A loose upper bound may grow without the bounded function growing with it.

What happens near the missing input? For 0<x<π/20<x<\pi/2, the unit-circle comparison in radians gives sinx<x<tanx\sin x<x<\tan x. Divide the first inequality by x>0x>0, and rewrite the second using tanx=sinx/cosx\tan x=\sin x/\cos x: cosx<sinxx<1.\cos x<\frac{\sin x}{x}<1. As xx approaches 00, the two outer quantities approach 11, so the middle quantity does too. Moreover, h(−x)=−sinx−x=h(x),h(-x)=\frac{-\sin x}{-x}=h(x), so the same conclusion holds from the left. Thus limx→0sinxx=1,\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1, and the graph has an open circle at (0,1)(0,1), not a vertical asymptote. Assigning the separate value h(0)=1h(0)=1 would produce a continuous extension; it would be a newly specified function with a larger domain.

Zeros and lobes. The zeros are x=nπx=n\pi for nonzero integers nn. There is no zero at 00, because the function is undefined there. On (0,π)(0,\pi) the graph is positive, on (π,2π)(\pi,2\pi) it is negative, and the signs alternate thereafter. Reflect these pieces in the vertical axis to obtain the negative half. Contact with one of the two envelopes occurs when |sinx|=1|\sin x|=1. Finally, the bounds ±1/|x|\pm1/|x| approach 00 as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, so the horizontal axis is an asymptote in both directions.

Locating the range more precisely. The upper endpoint is 11, approached but never attained. For 0<|x|<π/20<|x|<\pi/2, this follows from the unit-circle inequality above; for |x|≥π/2|x|\geq\pi/2, |h(x)|≤1/|x|≤2/π<1|h(x)|\leq1/|x|\leq2/\pi<1. The lowest point lies on the first negative lobe. Here is a precise way to specify it without guessing its location from a picture. On (π,2π)(\pi,2\pi), h′(x)=xcosx−sinxx2.h'(x)=\frac{x\cos x-\sin x}{x^2}. Put q(x)=xcosx−sinxq(x)=x\cos x-\sin x. Then q′(x)=−xsinx>0q'(x)=-x\sin x>0 on this interval, while q(π)=−π<0q(\pi)=-\pi<0 and q(3π/2)=1>0q(3\pi/2)=1>0. There is exactly one zero α∈(π,3π/2)\alpha\in(\pi,3\pi/2). At this input cosα≠0\cos\alpha\ne0, and q(α)=0q(\alpha)=0 is equivalent to tanα=α\tan\alpha=\alpha. The function decreases before α\alpha and increases after it, so its minimum on the lobe is m=sinα/αm=\sin\alpha/\alpha. No later lobe can go lower: for x≥2πx\geq2\pi, h(x)≥−12π>−23π=h(3π/2)≥m.h(x)\geq-\frac1{2\pi}>-\frac{2}{3\pi} =h(3\pi/2)\geq m. Evenness handles the negative half-axis. Hence the exact range is [sinαα,1),tanα=α,π<α<3π2.\left[\frac{\sin\alpha}{\alpha},1\right),\qquad \tan\alpha=\alpha,\quad \pi<\alpha<\frac{3\pi}{2}. Numerically, α≈4.49341\alpha\approx4.49341 and the lower endpoint is approximately −0.217234-0.217234. The graph construction itself needs only the zeros, the hole, the signs, the symmetry and the envelopes; the slope calculation additionally locates its global minimum.

Example 6.75

An exponentially damped oscillation

Sketch h(x)=e−xsinxh(x)=e^{-x}\sin x.

Solution.

The exponential factor is positive for every real input. Thus multiplying −1≤sinx≤1-1\leq\sin x\leq1 preserves the order: −e−x≤h(x)≤e−x.-e^{-x}\leq h(x)\leq e^{-x}. Draw the two envelopes y=e−xy=e^{-x} and y=−e−xy=-e^{-x}. The product is zero at every x=nπx=n\pi, and its sign is exactly the sign of sinx\sin x. It touches the upper envelope at x=π/2+2nπx=\pi/2+2n\pi, and the lower envelope at x=3π/2+2nπx=3\pi/2+2n\pi.

As xx increases, e−xe^{-x} shrinks; this is called damping. For example, moving forward by one full sine period gives h(x+2π)=e−(x+2π)sin(x+2π)=e−2πh(x).h(x+2\pi)=e^{-(x+2\pi)}\sin(x+2\pi)=e^{-2\pi}h(x). The heights are multiplied by e−2πe^{-2\pi}, a number strictly between 00 and 11. The zeros repeat, but the heights do not, so the product is not periodic.

On the negative half-axis the situation is reversed: e−xe^{-x} grows as xx moves to the left. A single vertical scale can make the right-hand oscillations almost invisible beside the large left-hand ones. We therefore use three windows of the same function.

The domain is ℝ\mathbb{R}. As x→∞x\to\infty, both bounds tend to 00, so h(x)→0h(x)\to0. This also rules out every possible positive period TT: periodicity would force h(π/2+nT)=h(π/2)>0h(\pi/2+nT)=h(\pi/2)>0 for every positive integer nn, whereas these inputs tend to infinity and their values must tend to zero. Towards the left, there is no limit: inputs π/2−2nπ\pi/2-2n\pi give positive values tending to ∞\infty, whereas inputs −π/2−2nπ-\pi/2-2n\pi give negative values tending to −∞-\infty. Following the unbroken curve between such points gives every intervening height. This graphical reading gives range ℝ\mathbb{R}; its formal continuity justification belongs to the Calculus module.

After the Calculus module: envelope contacts and turning points. Skip this derivative calculation on a first reading. It makes the geometric distinction explicit: h′(x)=e−x(cosx−sinx).h'(x)=e^{-x}(\cos x-\sin x). The turning points occur at x=π/4+nπx=\pi/4+n\pi, whereas envelope contacts occur at x=π/2+nπx=\pi/2+n\pi. For instance, the first positive maximum is at π/4\pi/4, before the sine factor reaches 11. The exponential factor has already been decreasing throughout that interval.

6.20 Bringing the Constructions Together

The position of a symbol matters. In f(|x|)f(|x|), the absolute value changes the input before the function is evaluated. In |f(x)||f(x)|, the function is evaluated first and its output is folded upwards. In |y|=f(x)|y|=f(x), we must solve for all possible yy. The three expressions answer different questions, even though they contain the same symbols.

💡 Solving for the vertical coordinate

For an allowed input xx, write c=f(x)c=f(x). Then equationwhen outputs existall possible outputs|y|=cc≥0y=c or y=−c⌊y⌋=cc∈ℤc≤y<c+1{y}=c0≤c<1y=n+c,n∈ℤ\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{equation}&\text{when outputs exist}&\text{all possible outputs}\\ \hline |y|=c&c\ge0&y=c\text{ or }y=-c\\[2pt] \lfloor y\rfloor=c&c\in\mathbb{Z}&c\le y<c+1\\[2pt] \{y\}=c&0\le c<1&y=n+c,\quad n\in\mathbb{Z} \end{array} At c=0c=0, the two modulus outputs coincide. The greatest-integer relation contains a whole half-open interval of heights. The fractional-part relation contains heights spaced one unit apart. A curve, a vertical segment and a family of curves must not be confused.

QuestionA useful starting point
Where does a point move?Solve for the new input, then evaluate the new output using the point map.
Which part is copied?Identify the input interval that remains before reflecting or periodically repeating it.
Where does a rule change?Locate zeros for modulus; integer levels for floor and fractional part; intersections for maximum and minimum.
What happens at a boundary?Substitute the boundary into the original formula. A limiting point need not belong to the graph.
What surrounds the curve?Find upper and lower envelopes, keeping the sign of every multiplier or denominator.
Does a sketch prove the claim?Use algebra, an interval argument or a monotonicity test to justify what the picture suggests.

Across these six lectures, we have learnt to read formulas as instructions about points, intervals and sets. Absolute value describes distance; functions organise inputs and outputs; symmetry and periodicity reduce the amount of a graph we must study; transformations let one familiar picture explain many others. This is the language we shall use when studying limits, continuity and change in Calculus.
